npcs.name: Ernesto "Paletta" Tarditi
npcs.title: Capostazione (retired)

lines: The 7:12 stopped again this morning. I raised the paddle and it stopped. Every morning I expect it not to.
Two passengers today! One of them was lost, but a passenger is a passenger.
The 10:40 intercity, 1987. A man threw his hat out of the window and shouted 'Casalrana!' as if it were a curse. I still have the hat.
Geometra! Mind the line. The trains don't stop here, but they do pass, and they pass with feeling.
I polish the paddle every morning. A station master without a polished paddle is just a man waving at trains.
Welcome, welcome! Ernesto Tarditi, Capostazione. Retired. Everyone calls me Paletta, after this.
You must be the Geometra! The province actually sent someone. I'll write and thank them. In triplicate.

sleepy: *yawn* The night express, 23:51. I can hear it in my sleep. I sleep through everything except trains.

topics.label: Why the paddle?
lines: The paletta! Red on one side, green on the other. You hold it up and the train goes. That was my whole job for thirty-one years.
The station went unmanned in 1993. They took the timetable off the wall and left me the paddle. An oversight, I think. I didn't remind them.

topics.label: Tell me about the petition.
lines: The railway says a stop needs two hundred and fifty signatures. Casalrana has forty-one inhabitants, counting the priest, who is shared with four other villages.
So we need the plain. The next villages, the bus, Matteo's whole school. Every good thing you do here, people talk about it, and then they sign. That's how the plain works.

topics.label: Which trains pass?
lines: Regionals, red and white, every hour or so. Intercity expresses, white and green, very proud of themselves. Freight trains as long as a sermon.
At night the express to the south. And at dawn, once, the yellow inspection train, checking the line. That's the one I salute properly.

gifts.line: From the railway's storeroom. The railway has forgotten it owns this wire. I haven't forgotten. Take it.

npcs.name: Battista "Barba Tista" Mosso
npcs.title: Fattore

lines: Herons. Eleven of them this morning, standing in my paddy like they're waiting for a bus. Brussels pays me for every one. I count them twice.
Clear skies again. Too clear. When the sky looks this innocent, it's planning something.
The tractor started first time today. I don't trust it.
Barba Tista. Uncle Tista. Everyone's uncle, nobody's nephew. What do you need?

sleepy: *mumble* ...four herons... five herons... Brussels, I'm counting...

topics.label: Is it true you grow herons?
lines: Brussels pays me to flood a paddy in winter so the birds have somewhere to stand. Herons, egrets, the lot. Money for water.
I didn't believe it either. I still don't. But the cheque came. The cheque is the most convincing bird of all.

topics.label: Who owns the farmstead?
lines: A count. Or a count's nephew. Somebody in Turin with a lawyer. Nobody's seen him since 1974.
I send the accounts every Christmas. Nobody answers. Fifty years of farming for an envelope.

topics.label: What's wrong with clear weather?
lines: Nothing. That's what's wrong with it. A December without fog? My father would have called the priest.
Mark my words. One morning you'll wake up and the plain will have gone. White, to the end of your nose. Then we'll talk.

gifts.line: Bits of the old thresher. It doesn't need them. It hasn't needed anything since 1979.

lines: I sat on my bench yesterday until the stars came out. My knees complained. My heart didn't.
Come in, come in, you're letting the cold in. Sit. Eat something. You're too thin for December.
Eighty-one years old and I still make the panissa for the whole village. The secret? Don't tell anyone the secret.
In 1951 I weeded these paddies with forty other girls, singing all day. My back remembers every one of those songs.

topics.label: What was it like, weeding the paddies?
lines: Water to your knees, the sun on your neck, and the boss on the bank in a straw hat. Forty days, from May into June.
We sang so we wouldn't cry, and then we sang because we liked it. I met my Gino on the bank there. He was terrible at weeding. Lovely singer.

topics.label: Where are all the frogs?
lines: Asleep in the mud, every one of them, until the spring. Like old men after lunch.
When I was a girl we ate them fried. Now I'd feel I was eating a neighbour. Let them sleep.

topics.label: What's in the panissa?
lines: Rice, beans, a little salami from the pot, onion, red wine, and patience.
The rest is a secret. Silvia has been trying to get it out of me for twenty years. She thinks I put it in a binder. I put it in my head.

gifts.line: Take these home. No, don't argue. I'm knitting you something too, in a colour I'll choose.

npcs.name: Silvia Bonino
npcs.title: Perita agraria

lines: Casalrana rice, husked at our own mill, in our own cloth bags. I printed the labels myself. They're slightly crooked. That's called 'artisanal'.
I went up the bell tower and my phone rang! Three messages from my college. They want their binder back.
Two years of agricultural college and Nonna still tells me how to plant cabbages. She's right, that's the annoying part.
I have a plan for this farmstead. I have a binder for the plan. I have a plan for the binder.
My mobile phone has no signal anywhere in Casalrana. I carry it for emotional reasons.

sleepy: *yawn* I was doing the accounts in my sleep. They balanced. It was a nightmare.

topics.label: Why restart the old mill?
lines: We grow rice and sell it to a cooperative that sells it to a factory that puts it in a box with a picture of a happy farmer.
I want to husk our own, put it in a cloth bag that says Casalrana, and sell it to people who'll come here to buy it. Then the farmer in the picture can be Uncle Tista. Unhappy, but real.

topics.label: Does your phone work anywhere?
lines: Not in the office, not in the yard, not on the road. I've walked every bank with it held over my head like a torch.
Uncle Tista says the plain is too flat for the signal to land. I don't think that's how it works. I don't know how it works.

topics.label: What did you study?
lines: Agriculture, in Vercelli. Soils, water, machinery, accounting. Everything Nonna knows, but with exams.
My final thesis was on the winter paddy for the birds. Uncle Tista read it. He said 'so it's true then' and went to count herons.

gifts.line: Two bags of our rice and some cloth bags. The first ones I sewed are lumpy. Those are for friends.

npcs.name: Don Remo Avetta
npcs.title: Parish priest

lines: The ox ate the manger's straw during the Gloria. Theologically interesting. Very lovely all the same.
Did you hear the bells this morning? I rang them myself. My arms will never forgive me, and my soul is delighted.
Ah, the Geometra! I cover five parishes on a motorbike older than you. Pray for my brakes.
The church of San Grato. Bare brick, no frescoes, very good acoustics. Even my sermons sound clever in here.
Bocce on Thursdays, Mass on Sundays. Don't tell the bishop which one I'm better at.

sleepy: *yawn* ...and the Lord said... no, that was the bishop...

topics.label: Why ring the bells by hand?
lines: The electric motor broke in 1998 and the diocese sent a form. I filled in the form. The form is still somewhere in Vercelli, ringing nothing.
Bells rung by hand sound different. You can hear the person pulling. For Christmas, I'd like Casalrana to hear its people.

topics.label: Five parishes?
lines: Casalrana and four others, all across the plain. Sunday is a race: Mass at eight here, nine-thirty at the next, eleven at the third.
The congregations average twelve. Twelve good people. The Lord started with twelve, so I'm in good company.

topics.label: Is it true you play bocce?
lines: Who told you? Nonna Pierina. Of course.
I was provincial champion in 1983, before the seminary. I still play on Thursdays, in a cap, at a club where nobody knows I'm a priest. They think I'm a very calm accountant.

gifts.line: Hellebores from the churchyard wall, and something from the collection box. The parish council approved it. I am the parish council.

lines: I'm going to school by train now! Well, I could. Mum still drives me. But I COULD.
The 14:20 intercity was four minutes late! I wrote it down. Somebody has to.
I'm Paletta's staff. He says I'm the best staff he ever had. I'm the only staff he ever had, but still.
Grandpa says if I count trains instead of doing homework I'll end up a station master. That's the PLAN.

topics.label: What's in your notebook?
lines: Every train since I came to stay with Grandpa. Number, time, colour, and if anyone waved.
Seventeen people waved. Two of them were the same lady. I think she likes Casalrana.

topics.label: Why are you staying with your grandpa?
lines: Mum and Dad work in the city till Christmas. They phone every Sunday from the payphone at the station, because Silvia's phone is useless.
Grandpa lets me drive the tractor in the yard. Don't tell Mum. Actually, tell her, she'll be impressed.

topics.label: What's your museum?
lines: A shelf in the waiting room. Paletta said I could have it. It's got a railway ticket from 1962, a horseshoe and a rock that looks like Italy.
It needs more exhibits. Real old things. Things with stories.

gifts.line: This is for you. It's a thing somebody dropped from the 16:05. It's mine, so now it's yours. That's how gifts work.

lines: Pautasso, railway inspection. I have a clipboard and a thermos, and I'm not afraid to use either.
Conditions are conditions, Geometra. I don't make the rules. I just write them down very neatly.
